Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Fix $n \ge 1$
and write
$$S^{n-1}:=\{\omega \in \mathbb R^n : |\omega|=1\}.$$
Let
$$\Phi:\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}\longrightarrow(0,\infty)\times S^{n-1},\qquad \Phi(x)=(|x|,x/|x|).$$
This map is continuous. If $E\subseteq S^{n-1}$ is Borel, then
$(0,1]\times E$ is Borel and
$$\{r\omega:\omega\in E,\ 0<r\le1\}=\Phi^{-1}((0,1]\times E)$$
is Borel in $\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$ by
[[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]], hence Borel in
$\mathbb R^n$ by [[thm-borel-sigma-algebra-of-a-subspace-is-the-trace]]. It is
therefore Lebesgue measurable by [[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]].
Define
$$\sigma(E):=n\,\lambda_n(\{r\omega : \omega \in E,\ 0<r\le 1\}).$$

The next theorem proves that this is a Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ and that it
is exactly the surface measure needed for polar coordinates.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n \ge 1$,
let $S^{n-1} \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be the unit sphere, and let $\sigma$ be the
set function of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. Then $\sigma$
is a finite Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$, and for every Borel measurable
$f : \mathbb R^n \to [0,\infty]$,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n} f(x)\,d\lambda_n(x) = \int_0^\infty \int_{S^{n-1}} f(r\omega) r^{n-1}\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dr.$$
Moreover, $\sigma$ is the unique Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ with this
property.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ and $n\ge2$. The chart surface measure on $S^{n-1}$ equals the polar measure $\sigma$. Orthogonal transformations preserve it. The map $\omega\mapsto a+R\omega$, $R>0$, multiplies surface measure by $R^{n-1}$, and $|S^{n-1}|=n|B_1|$.

A **compact Jordan parameter region** is a compact Jordan measurable set $D\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ that is the closure of its nonempty connected interior $D^\circ$ ([[def-riemann-integral-over-a-jordan-set]], [[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]]). Its boundary has content zero ([[thm-jordan-boundary-criterion]]).

A regular parametrized surface patch is the image of a $C^1$ map from a compact Jordan parameter region whose parameter cross product is nonzero on the region's interior and for which no interior parameter point shares its image with a distinct point of the whole region. Seam identifications and rank failures may occur only on the boundary. Here $C^1$ is the Euclidean componentwise class of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. More precisely, the parametrization $\varphi$ is defined on an open neighbourhood of $D$, $\varphi_u\times\varphi_v\ne0$ on $D^\circ$, and no point of $D^\circ$ has the same image as a distinct point of $D$. The chosen pair $(D,\varphi)$ is part of the patch data.

Let $(D,\varphi)$ be a regular surface patch and let $q$ be a continuous real-valued function on $\varphi[D]$. For a continuous scalar field $q$ on the patch image, $\int_Sq\,dS:=\int_D(q\circ\varphi)J_\varphi$, and $\operatorname{Area}(S):=\int_DJ_\varphi$.

Here $S$ denotes the patch with its chosen parametrization. Both integrands are bounded and Riemann integrable on the compact Jordan region $D$ by continuity ([[thm-continuous-functions-on-compact-jordan-sets-are-integrable]]). Boundary values are included in the parameter integral but may be changed on the content-zero boundary without changing its value.

For every parameter point, $J_\varphi=\|\varphi_u\times\varphi_v\|_2$.

The common value is positive in the interior of a regular patch; it may vanish on the parameter boundary under the admitted seam and endpoint convention.

Changing a bounded scalar or flux parameter integrand only on the content-zero boundary of a compact Jordan parameter region preserves integrability and its integral.

In both directions, one of the two bounded functions is integrable if and only if the other is, and then their integrals agree.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on the closed bounded interval $[a,b]$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-continuity-real]]), and let $y \in \mathbb{R}$ satisfy

$$f(a) \le y \le f(b) \qquad \text{or} \qquad f(b) \le y \le f(a) .$$

Then there is $c \in [a,b]$ with $f(c) = y$.

**The construction is canonical, so no choice principle is used.** The bisection
below tests the left half first and takes the right half only when the left one
has been ruled out, so the passage from one interval to the next is a *function*
of that interval, and [[thm-recursion]] applies with nothing selected. This is
the same discipline the library uses wherever a sequence is built one term at a
time.

**Completeness of $\mathbb{R}$ is what does the work.** The bisection produces a
nested sequence of closed bounded intervals whose lengths tend to $0$, and it is
[[thm-nested-interval-property]] — hence the least-upper-bound property — that
supplies the point. Over an ordered field that is not complete the theorem
fails; the witness for that, stated for an arbitrary ordered field and worked
over $\mathbb{Q}$, is
[[cex-evt-and-ivt-fail-over-a-non-complete-field]], which states its own
$\varepsilon$-$\delta$ continuity inline and is not an instance of this page's
definition.

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad\cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x,\quad\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x.$$
In particular,
$$\sin(\pi/2)=1,\quad\cos(\pi/2)=0,\quad\sin\pi=0,\quad\cos\pi=-1.$$

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(-x)=-\sin x,\qquad\cos(-x)=\cos x,\qquad\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1.$$
Consequently $|\sin x|\le1$ and $|\cos x|\le1$.

Sine is strictly increasing on each interval $[-\pi/2+2m\pi,\pi/2+2m\pi]$ and strictly decreasing on each interval $[\pi/2+2m\pi,3\pi/2+2m\pi]$. Cosine is strictly decreasing on $[2m\pi,(2m+1)\pi]$ and strictly increasing on $[(2m+1)\pi,(2m+2)\pi]$. Both functions have range $[-1,1]$.

For all real $x,y$,
$$\sin(x+y)=\sin x\cos y+\cos x\sin y,$$
$$\cos(x+y)=\cos x\cos y-\sin x\sin y.$$

For every real $x$,
$$\sin x=0\Longleftrightarrow x=m\pi\text{ for some }m\in\mathbb Z,\qquad \cos x=0\Longleftrightarrow x=(m+1/2)\pi\text{ for some }m\in\mathbb Z.$$
Both sine and cosine have period $2\pi$, and no smaller positive number is a common period.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]), let $F$ be its integral function
([[def-the-integral-function]]), and let $c \in [a,b]$ be a point at which $f$ is
continuous ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $F$ is differentiable at $c$ as a
function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]) and

$$F'(c) \;=\; f(c) .$$

At $c = a$ and $c = b$ this is the one-sided statement, which is what
[[def-derivative]] means at those points: every point of a nondegenerate interval
is a limit point of it, so $F'(c)$ is a meaningful symbol at every $c \in [a,b]$,
and the difference quotient is taken over $[a,b] \setminus \{c\}$.

**Consequently, if $f$ is continuous on the whole of $[a,b]$, then $F$ is a
primitive of $f$ there**: $F' = f$ at every point of $[a,b]$.

**Continuity at $c$ is a hypothesis and it cannot be dropped.** For an integrable
$f$ that is discontinuous at $c$, $F'(c)$ may fail to exist, and it may exist and
differ from $f(c)$; both are exhibited on the companion page, by
an integrable function with no primitive and by a false
statement about the integral function.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.
For all $u,v,w\in\mathbb R^3$, the cross product is bilinear and alternating, $\langle u\times v,w\rangle=\det[u\ v\ w]$, and $u\times v$ is orthogonal to both $u$ and $v$.

For $u,v\in\mathbb R^3$, $\|u\times v\|_2^2=\det G(u,v)$, and this value is positive exactly when $u$ and $v$ are linearly independent.

Equivalently,
$$\|u\times v\|_2^2=\|u\|_2^2\|v\|_2^2-\langle u,v\rangle^2.$$

Let $k\in\mathbb N$. Finite componentwise sums and products of $C^k$ Euclidean maps are $C^k$, and a composite of composable $C^k$ Euclidean maps is $C^k$. Scalar multiples are included among the finite componentwise operations. The assertions remain valid on an empty open domain.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

Let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable. Its positive and negative parts are
$$f^+:=\max\{f,0\},\qquad f^-:=\max\{-f,0\};$$
they are measurable by
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]] and
satisfy $f=f^+-f^-$ and $|f|=f^++f^-$.

The **Lebesgue integral of a real measurable function** is defined whenever at
most one of $\int f^+\,d\mu$ and $\int f^-\,d\mu$ is $+\infty$, in which case
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\int f^+\,d\mu-\int f^-\,d\mu.$$
The function is **integrable** when both integrals are finite, equivalently
when $\int|f|\,d\mu<+\infty$.

For a complex measurable function $h=u+iv$ with
$u=\operatorname{Re}h,\ v=\operatorname{Im}h$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]), define $h$ to be
**integrable** when $|h|$ is integrable, and then define
$$\int h\,d\mu:=\int u\,d\mu+i\int v\,d\mu.$$

Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

Let $E\subseteq\mathbb R^{p+q}$ be a bounded Jordan set and let $g:E\to\mathbb R$ be Riemann integrable. Suppose that for all $x$ outside a content-zero set $N\subseteq\mathbb R^p$, the section $E_x$ is Jordan measurable and $g_x$ is integrable over it. Put $h(x)=\int_{E_x}g_x$ there and assign arbitrary bounded values to $h$ on $N$, with empty-section integral equal to $0$. Then $h$ is integrable on any rectangle containing the projection of $E$, its integral is independent of that rectangle and of the values on $N$, and
$$\int_Eg=\int h(x)\,dx.$$
The symmetric assertion holds for the other coordinate block.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $n\ge1$ and let $\sigma$ be the polar surface measure on the unit sphere $S^{n-1}\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ ([[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]). Then the reflection $R\omega=-\omega$ preserves $\sigma$, and the first moment vanishes:
$$\int_{S^{n-1}}\omega\,d\sigma(\omega)=0\in\mathbb R^n,\qquad\text{so}\qquad \int_{S^{n-1}}a\cdot\omega\,d\sigma(\omega)=0\quad(a\in\mathbb R^n).$$
The integrals are finite because $\sigma$ is a finite Borel measure.
For every $n\ge1$, $V_n(1)=\pi^{n/2}/\Gamma(n/2+1)$. Here $n$ is an integer.
For every $s>0$, $\Gamma(s+1)=s\Gamma(s)$, and $\Gamma(1)=1$.
$\Gamma(1/2)=\sqrt\pi$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. If $f : V \to \mathbb C$ belongs to $L^1(\lambda_n)$,
then
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be
$C^1$, and let $a\in U$.  If $Df(a)$ is invertible, then there are open sets
$V,W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $a\in V\subseteq U$ and $f(a)\in W$ such that
$f|_V:V\to W$ is bijective.  Its inverse $g:W\to V$ is $C^1$, and

$$Dg(y)=Df(g(y))^{-1}\qquad(y\in W).$$

Thus $f$ is a local diffeomorphism at $a$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$m,n \ge 1$. Under the identification
$$\mathbb R^{m+n}=\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n,$$
the product measure $\lambda_m \times \lambda_n$ and the Euclidean Lebesgue
measure $\lambda_{m+n}$ agree on every Borel subset of $\mathbb R^{m+n}$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of [[def-half-open-box]], and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $n\ge1$, let $Q=\prod_{j=1}^n[a_j,b_j]$ with $a_j<b_j$, and let $f:Q\to\mathbb R$ be bounded and Borel. If $f$ is Riemann integrable, then $f\in L^1(\lambda_n|_Q)$ and its Lebesgue and Riemann integrals agree.

derivations.claim: Define $X(\theta,\varphi):=(\sin\theta\cos\varphi,\ \sin\theta\sin\varphi,\ \cos\theta)$ and $D:=[0,\pi]\times[0,2\pi]$. Then $D$ is a compact Jordan parameter region, being a closed bounded rectangle and the closure of its nonempty connected interior $D^\circ=(0,\pi)\times(0,2\pi)$, and $X$ is $C^1$ on the open neighbourhood $\mathbb R^2$ of $D$ because its components are finite sums and products of the $C^1$ functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ [F5, F8]. Its partial derivatives are $X_\theta=(\cos\theta\cos\varphi,\cos\theta\sin\varphi,-\sin\theta)$ and $X_\varphi=(-\sin\theta\sin\varphi,\sin\theta\cos\varphi,0)$, and the coordinate formula for the cross product gives $$X_\theta\times X_\varphi=(\sin^{2}\theta\cos\varphi,\ \sin^{2}\theta\sin\varphi,\ \sin\theta\cos\theta)=\sin\theta\,X(\theta,\varphi),$$ since $\cos^{2}\varphi+\sin^{2}\varphi=1$; also $|X(\theta,\varphi)|^{2}=\sin^{2}\theta+\cos^{2}\theta=1$ [F5, F7]. Hence $X_\theta\times X_\varphi=0$ exactly when $\sin\theta=0$; on the interior $\theta\in(0,\pi)$ one has $\sin\theta>0$ by strict monotonicity and the values $\sin0=\sin\pi=0$ [F5], so the parameter cross product is nonzero on $D^\circ$.

The chart covers the sphere and is injective in its interior. If $n\in S^2$, the intermediate value theorem between the endpoint values $\cos0=1$, $\cos\pi=-1$, and strict monotonicity of cosine on $[0,\pi]$ gives a unique $\theta\in[0,\pi]$ with $\cos\theta=n_3$, so $\sin\theta=\bigl(n_1^{2}+n_2^{2}\bigr)^{1/2}$ because $\sin\theta\ge0$ on $[0,\pi]$ and $\sin^{2}\theta=1-\cos^{2}\theta$ [F5]. If $\sin\theta=0$ then $n=\pm e_3=X(0,0)$ or $X(\pi,0)$; otherwise put $c:=n_1/\sin\theta$ and $s:=n_2/\sin\theta$, so $c^{2}+s^{2}=1$, and choose $\varphi\in[0,\pi]$ with $\cos\varphi=c$ when $s\ge0$ and $\varphi\in[\pi,2\pi]$ with $\cos\varphi=c$ when $s<0$, possible because cosine has range $[-1,1]$ and is strictly monotone on each interval; then $\sin\varphi$ has the sign of $s$ there and $\sin^{2}\varphi=1-c^{2}=s^{2}$, so $\sin\varphi=s$ and $n=X(\theta,\varphi)$. Thus $X[D]=S^2$. Conversely, if $X(\theta,\varphi)=X(\theta',\varphi')$ with $(\theta,\varphi)\in D^\circ$ and $(\theta',\varphi')\in D$, then $\cos\theta=\cos\theta'$ with both angles in $[0,\pi]$, so $\theta=\theta'$ by strict monotonicity; then $\sin\theta>0$ and the first two coordinates give $\cos\varphi=\cos\varphi'$ and $\sin\varphi=\sin\varphi'$, hence $\cos(\varphi-\varphi')=\cos\varphi\cos\varphi'+\sin\varphi\sin\varphi'=\cos^{2}\varphi+\sin^{2}\varphi=1$ [F5]. Writing $x:=\varphi-\varphi'\in(-2\pi,2\pi)$ and using $\cos x=1-2\sin^{2}(x/2)$, we get $\sin(x/2)=0$, so $x/2=m\pi$ for some integer $m$ and $x=2m\pi$; since $|x|<2\pi$ this forces $x=0$, that is $\varphi=\varphi'$ [F5]. Therefore no interior parameter point shares its image with a distinct point of $D$, and $(D,X)$ is a regular parametrized surface patch with image $S^2$.

Reduction to the chart, including its seam and poles. Let $q:S^2\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. Put $H:=\{y\in\mathbb R^3:y_2=0,\ y_1\ge0\}$ and $Y(r,\theta,\varphi):=rX(\theta,\varphi)$ on $U:=(0,1)\times D^\circ$. By step 2.1, $Y$ is a bijection from $U$ onto the open set $V:=B_1(0)\setminus H$. Its derivative has columns $X,rX_\theta,rX_\varphi$, so $\det DY=r^2X\cdot(X_\theta\times X_\varphi)=r^2\sin\theta>0$ by step 1.1. The local inverse theorem [F13] makes its bijective inverse $C^1$ locally at every point, hence $Y$ is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism. The omitted set $H\cap B_1$ is contained in the degenerate box $[-1,1]\times\{0\}\times[-1,1]$ and is Lebesgue null by [F13]. The bounded Borel function $q(y/|y|)$ on $B_1\setminus\{0\}$, assigned zero at $0$, is integrable by [F13]. Applying the polar formula of [[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]] to its positive and negative parts gives $\int_{B_1}q(y/|y|)dy=\tfrac13\int_{S^2}q\,d\sigma$. Change of variables by $Y$ and Fubini [F13] give the same integral as $\int_0^1r^2dr\int_{D^\circ}q(X(\theta,\varphi))\sin\theta\,d\theta d\varphi$. The parameter boundary is a finite union of degenerate boxes and therefore null; the integrand extends continuously to $D$, and its Lebesgue integral equals its Riemann integral by [F13]. Cancelling $\int_0^1r^2dr=1/3$ therefore proves $$\int_{S^2}q\,d\sigma=\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\pi q(X(\theta,\varphi))\sin\theta\,d\theta d\varphi.$$ This supplies the measure identification despite the seam and pole degeneracies; it does not apply an injective regular atlas chart across those degeneracies. In particular, for $q=f\circ n_3$, $n_3\circ X=\cos\theta$ gives $I:=\int_{S^2}f(n_3)d\sigma=\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\pi f(\cos\theta)\sin\theta\,d\theta d\varphi$.

Conclusion of (a). The function $g(\theta,\varphi):=f(\cos\theta)\sin\theta$ is continuous on the rectangle $D$ [F5, F8], hence Riemann integrable, and its sections in $\varphi$ are continuous; [F10] therefore gives $I=\int_0^{\pi}\bigl(\int_0^{2\pi}f(\cos\theta)\sin\theta\,d\varphi\bigr)d\theta=2\pi\int_0^{\pi}f(\cos\theta)\sin\theta\,d\theta$. Let $P(u):=\int_{-1}^{u}f(v)\,dv$ on $[-1,1]$; by [F6] $P'=f$, and the chain rule [F6] with $\cos'=-\sin$ [F5] gives $(P\circ\cos)'(\theta)=-f(\cos\theta)\sin\theta$ on $[0,\pi]$. Since this derivative is continuous, the second fundamental theorem [F6] applies and $$\int_0^{\pi}f(\cos\theta)\sin\theta\,d\theta=-\bigl[P(\cos\theta)\bigr]_0^{\pi}=P(1)-P(-1)=\int_{-1}^{1}f(u)\,du,$$ because $\cos0=1$ and $\cos\pi=-1$ [F5]. Combining with step 3.1 gives $\int_{S^2}f(n_3)\,d\sigma=2\pi\int_{-1}^{1}f(u)\,du$, which is (a); all integrands here are continuous on the compact sets in question, so the displayed integrals are finite.

Conclusion of (b). Let $\eta_1(n_1,n_2,n_3):=(-n_1,n_2,n_3)$ and $\eta_2(n_1,n_2,n_3):=(n_1,-n_2,n_3)$. Each is an orthogonal bijection of $\mathbb R^3$ with $\eta_i[S^2]=S^2$, so each preserves $\sigma$ [F2]; by the substitution identity of [F11], applied to the bounded Borel function $g_i(n):=n_if(n_3)$ and the fact that $g_i\circ\eta_i=-g_i$, we get $\int_{S^2}n_if(n_3)\,d\sigma=-\int_{S^2}n_if(n_3)\,d\sigma$, whence $\int_{S^2}n_if(n_3)\,d\sigma=0$ for $i=1,2$ (finiteness of both integrals is [F9]). For the third component, (a) applied to the continuous function $u\mapsto uf(u)$ gives $\int_{S^2}n_3f(n_3)\,d\sigma=2\pi\int_{-1}^{1}uf(u)\,du$. Since $n\cdot a=a_1n_1+a_2n_2+a_3n_3$, linearity of the $\sigma$-integral [F9] gives $$\int_{S^2}(n\cdot a)f(n_3)\,d\sigma=2\pi\,a_3\int_{-1}^{1}uf(u)\,du,$$ which is (b).

Conclusion of (c). Expanding the square, $(n\cdot a)^{2}=\sum_{i,j=1}^{3}a_ia_jn_in_j$, and by linearity [F9] the integral is the finite sum $\sum_{i,j}a_ia_j\int_{S^2}n_in_jf(n_3)\,d\sigma$. For $i\ne j$ the function $n_in_jf(n_3)$ changes sign under $\eta_i$ (or $\eta_j$), so the substitution identity of [F11] gives $\int_{S^2}n_in_jf(n_3)\,d\sigma=0$. For the diagonal terms, the swap $\eta_3(n_1,n_2,n_3):=(n_2,n_1,n_3)$ is orthogonal and preserves $\sigma$ [F2], so the substitution identity gives $\int_{S^2}n_1^{2}f(n_3)\,d\sigma=\int_{S^2}n_2^{2}f(n_3)\,d\sigma$; with $n_1^{2}+n_2^{2}=1-n_3^{2}$ [F5] and linearity, $$2\int_{S^2}n_1^{2}f(n_3)\,d\sigma=\int_{S^2}\bigl(1-n_3^{2}\bigr)f(n_3)\,d\sigma=2\pi\int_{-1}^{1}(1-u^{2})f(u)\,du$$ by (a) applied to the continuous function $u\mapsto(1-u^{2})f(u)$; and (a) applied to $u\mapsto u^{2}f(u)$ gives $\int_{S^2}n_3^{2}f(n_3)\,d\sigma=2\pi\int_{-1}^{1}u^{2}f(u)\,du$. Substituting into the expansion yields $$\int_{S^2}(n\cdot a)^{2}f(n_3)\,d\sigma=2\pi\,a_3^{2}\int_{-1}^{1}u^{2}f(u)\,du+\pi\,(a_1^{2}+a_2^{2})\int_{-1}^{1}(1-u^{2})f(u)\,du,$$ which is (c).

Conclusion of (d) and scope (e). Taking $f=1$ in (a) gives $\sigma(S^2)=2\pi\int_{-1}^{1}du=4\pi$; independently [F2] gives $\sigma(S^2)=3|B_1|=3V_3(1)$, and [F12] evaluates $V_3(1)=\pi^{3/2}/\Gamma(5/2)$ with $\Gamma(5/2)=(3/2)(1/2)\Gamma(1/2)=3\sqrt\pi/4$, so $V_3(1)=4\pi/3$ and the two routes agree. Taking $f=1$ in (b) gives $\int_{S^2}(n\cdot a)\,d\sigma=0$ for every $a$, hence $\int_{S^2}n\,d\sigma=0$, and taking $f=1$ in (c) gives $\int_{S^2}(n\cdot a)^{2}d\sigma=2\pi a_3^{2}\cdot\tfrac{2}{3}+\pi(a_1^{2}+a_2^{2})\cdot\tfrac{4}{3}=\tfrac{4\pi}{3}|a|^{2}$; choosing $a=e_i$ and $a=e_i+e_j$ for $i\ne j$ reads off $\int_{S^2}n_i^{2}\,d\sigma=4\pi/3$ and $\int_{S^2}n_in_j\,d\sigma=0$ for $i\ne j$, that is $\int_{S^2}n_in_j\,d\sigma=(4\pi/3)\delta_{ij}$. Finally the norm identity of [F7] gives $|n\times a|^{2}=|n|^{2}|a|^{2}-(n\cdot a)^{2}=|a|^{2}-(n\cdot a)^{2}$ for $n\in S^2$, so by linearity [F9] and the value just computed $\int_{S^2}|n\times a|^{2}\,d\sigma=4\pi|a|^{2}-\tfrac{4\pi}{3}|a|^{2}=\tfrac{8\pi}{3}|a|^{2}$. This proves all identities of (d); every integrand is continuous on the compact $S^2$ and $\sigma$ is a finite Borel measure by [F1], so the integrals are absolutely convergent, $f$ need not be nonnegative, and no physical interpretation is asserted, which is (e).

citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), used through the sphere and polar integrations below ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]], [[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]]). Let $c>0$, write $Q:=\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$, $\mathcal D:=\mathcal D(Q)$ for the test-function space of [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]], and $C:=\{(y,t)\in Q:t=|y|/c\}$ for the retarded cone. Define the functional $K$ on test functions by

$$\langle K,\psi\rangle:=\frac{1}{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{\psi(y,|y|/c)}{|y|}\,dy\qquad(\psi\in\mathcal D).$$

Then: (a) the integral converges absolutely for every $\psi\in\mathcal D$, the functional $K$ is a distribution on $Q$ ([[def-distribution]]), $(K,\psi)=0$ for every $\psi$ with $\operatorname{supp}\psi\cap C=\varnothing$, and for every $(y_0,t_0)\in C$ and every neighbourhood $U$ of $(y_0,t_0)$ there is $\psi\in\mathcal D$ with $\operatorname{supp}\psi\subseteq U$ and $\langle K,\psi\rangle\ne0$; consequently $\operatorname{supp}K=C$. (b) For every $h\in C_c^\infty(Q)$ the function

$$(K*h)(x,t):=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{h(y,\,t-|x-y|/c)}{4\pi\,|x-y|}\,dy$$

is well defined (the integral converges absolutely), of class $C^\infty$ on $Q$, and for every $\psi\in\mathcal D$

$$\langle K*h,\psi\rangle=\langle h,\,K\circledast\psi\rangle,\qquad (K\circledast\psi)(y,s):=\langle K,\psi(y+\cdot,s+\cdot)\rangle=\frac{1}{4\pi}\int\frac{\psi(y+z,s+|z|/c)}{|z|}\,dz;$$

moreover $W(K*h)=h$ on $Q$ in the classical pointwise sense, where $W=c^{-2}\partial_t^2-\Delta$ is the wave expression of [[def-wave-equation-cauchy-data-and-wave-speed]] and [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]. (c) Read $W=c^{-2}\partial_t^2-\Delta$ as the distributional operator built from [[def-distributional-derivative]]; then $WK=\delta_{(0,0)}$ in the sense of [[def-dirac-delta-and-its-derivatives]], that is, $(WK)(\psi)=\psi(0,0)$ for every $\psi\in\mathcal D$. This identifies $K$ as the retarded fundamental solution of $W$; no smoothness of $K$ itself on the cone is asserted, and the advanced fundamental solution is not treated.

Adopt as a physical postulate of this framework the following four equations for
the fields of [[def-em-fields]] and the sources of [[def-em-sources]] on the
laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with
$\mu_0>0$, $c>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ and the SI units of
[[def-em-si-conventions]].

(a) [Smooth branch] Let $E,B$ be jointly $C^1$ fields with the additional
derivatives required by each equation existing and continuous, and let
$\rho,J$ be continuous. Then, with the divergence and curl of
[[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and the partial derivative
$\partial_t$ at fixed position of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]],

$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE.$$

(b) [Weak branch] Let instead $E,B$ be locally integrable $\mathbb R^3$-valued
fields and $\rho,J$ locally integrable scalar and vector fields on
$I\times\Omega$, identified with their regular distributions
([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]],
[[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]). Let
$\operatorname{div}$, $\operatorname{curl}$ and $\partial_t$ act as
distributional derivatives, componentwise, and let $\psi$ range over
$C_c^\infty(I\times\Omega)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]).
Then the same four identities hold in the sense of [[def-distribution]]: the
pairings

$$\langle\operatorname{div}E-\rho/\varepsilon_0,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{div}B,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{curl}E+\partial_tB,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{curl}B-\mu_0J-c^{-2}\partial_tE,\psi\rangle$$

all vanish for every such $\psi$, all derivatives being distributional
derivatives ([[def-distributional-derivative]]).

(c) [Scope] The postulate contains no magnetic charge: $\operatorname{div}B=0$
and no magnetic-source term appears in $\operatorname{curl}E$. Sources that
are not locally integrable functions (point or sheet sources) are covered by
neither branch and require their own definition. The equations are adopted
classical vacuum physics in the named inertial chart; they are not deduced from
charge conservation, from empirical agreement or from the special-relativity
postulates, and this item by itself asserts no covariance under changes of
inertial frame.

Let $c>0$ and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ be open. A **scalar-vector potential pair** of class $C^k$ on $\Omega$, for an integer $k\ge1$, is a pair $(\varphi,A)$ with $\varphi:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ and $A:\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ each of class $C^k$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], the components of $A$ being of class $C^k$ separately; the pair is **smooth** when both members are $C^\infty$, and **continuous**, or of class $C^0$, when both members are continuous. A pair defined on a set of the form $\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T]$ with $t_0<T$ is of class $C^k$, $k\ge1$, **in the extension sense** when there are an open interval $J\supset[t_0,T]$ and a potential pair of class $C^k$ on the open set $\mathbb R^3\times J$ whose restriction to $\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T]$ the given pair is; the same wording is used for $C^\infty$ and for the single functions $\varphi$ and $\chi$ below.

All operators $\nabla$, $\operatorname{div}$, $\operatorname{curl}$ and $\Delta$ below act on the three spatial coordinates with $t$ fixed: for $\Omega_t:=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:(x,t)\in\Omega\}$, apply the cited three-dimensional operators to the restrictions $x\mapsto\varphi(x,t)$, $x\mapsto A(x,t)$ or $x\mapsto u(x,t)$ on the open set $\Omega_t$. In particular $\nabla\varphi=(\partial_{x_1}\varphi,\partial_{x_2}\varphi,\partial_{x_3}\varphi)$ and $\Delta u=\sum_{i=1}^3\partial_{x_i}^2u$; $\partial_t$ differentiates only the time coordinate.

For a potential pair of class $C^k$ with $k\ge1$ its **electric field** and **magnetic field** are

$$E(\varphi,A):=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA,\qquad B(\varphi,A):=\operatorname{curl}A,$$

where $\nabla$ is the gradient of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]], $\partial_t$ is the partial derivative of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], and $\operatorname{div}$ and $\operatorname{curl}$ are those of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]. Both $E(\varphi,A)$ and $B(\varphi,A)$ are maps $\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^{k-1}$.

For $k\ge1$ the **Lorenz divergence** of the pair is the function

$$G(\varphi,A):=\operatorname{div}A+c^{-2}\partial_t\varphi,$$

also of class $C^{k-1}$, and the pair is **in Lorenz gauge** on $\Omega$ when $G(\varphi,A)=0$ throughout $\Omega$.

For $k\ge2$ and a function $\chi:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ of class $C^k$, a **gauge function**, the **gauge transform** of the pair is

$$T_{\chi}(\varphi,A):=(\varphi-\partial_t\chi,\ A+\nabla\chi),$$

again a potential pair, of class $C^{k-1}$.

Finally, for a function $u:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ of class $C^2$ put

$$Wu:=c^{-2}\partial_t^2u-\Delta u,$$

with $\Delta$ the Laplacian of [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]] and $\partial_t^2$ the second partial derivative in $t$ ([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]); this is the normalization $W=c^{-2}\Box_c$ of the wave operator $\Box_c=\partial_t^2-c^2\Delta$ of speed $c$ of [[def-wave-equation-cauchy-data-and-wave-speed]]. For a map $U:\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$ of class $C^2$ with components $U_1,\dots,U_m$, one writes $WU:=(WU_1,\dots,WU_m)$ componentwise.

Nothing in this definition asserts that a gauge function with prescribed auxiliary data exists, that every potential pair is gauge equivalent to a pair in Lorenz gauge, or that $Wu=g$ is solvable: those are conclusions with their own hypotheses. The signs $-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $A+\nabla\chi$, the factor $c^{-2}$ in $G$, and the spelling *Lorenz* are part of the convention.

Let the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$, its spatial Euclidean structure
and its units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and
[[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $k\ge1$. An **electric field of class
$C^k$** on the region is a map $E:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that is of class
$C^k$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; a
**magnetic field of class $C^k$** is a map $B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of
the same class. At fixed $t\in I$ the maps $E(\cdot,t),B(\cdot,t):\Omega\to
\mathbb R^3$ are real spatial vector fields on the region $\Omega$, read in the
$\delta$-orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the frame. The framework uses:
$C^1$ fields in the classical Maxwell branch, $C^2$ fields where second or
mixed time-space derivatives of the fields appear, and $C^\infty$ fields in
the smooth existence branches; every statement carries its own regularity and
no regularity beyond it is asserted.

Conventions:

(a) The **polar-vector** and **axial-vector** conventions mean the following
component rules under a spatial orthogonal coordinate change $y'=Qy$, where
$Q$ is a real $3\times3$ matrix with $Q^{\mathsf T}Q=I_3$. Transpose,
matrix product and identity are those of [[def-transpose-of-a-matrix]] and
[[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]], and $\det Q$ is the determinant
of [[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]. At corresponding
points $E'(y',t)=QE(y,t)$ and $B'(y',t)=(\det Q)QB(y,t)$. Thus polar and axial
components agree in their transformation rule when $\det Q=1$ and differ by
a sign when $\det Q=-1$. These rules specify the orientation convention;
the adopted inertial descriptions have positive orientation, and no physical
orientation-reversing change of description is adopted here.

(b) The fields are defined by their values on $\Omega\times I$, and no value at
a point of singular source support is asserted.

(c) $E$ carries V m$^{-1}$ and $B$ carries T.

(d) The identification of the pair $(E,B)$ with the components of an
alternating two-form, including its transformation behaviour, is made in the
framework's electromagnetic two-form definition on this page and is not
presupposed here.

Let $c>0$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with at least two elements ([[def-interval]]), and let $(\varphi,A)$ be a potential pair of class $C^2$ jointly on $\Omega\times I$ in the restriction convention of [[lem-em-joint-smooth-potentials]] ([[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]]): for open $I$ this is the ordinary open-domain class of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], and for non-open $I$ the pair is the restriction of a $C^2$ pair on an open neighbourhood of $\Omega\times I$, with relative derivatives at included endpoints and no time jet beyond the restricted values. Write $(E,B)$ for the field pair of $(\varphi,A)$ ([[def-em-fields]]) and

$$G:=\operatorname{div}A+c^{-2}\partial_t\varphi,\qquad W:=c^{-2}\partial_t^2-\Delta$$

for the Lorenz divergence and the wave expression of [[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]], with $\Delta$ the Laplacian of [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]. Let $\rho:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$ and $J:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be continuous source fields of the framework ([[def-em-sources]]).

(a) [Exact identities] Independently of any field equation,

$$\operatorname{div}E=W\varphi-\partial_tG,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B-c^{-2}\partial_tE=WA+\nabla G\qquad\text{on }\Omega\times I.$$

Consequently the sourced Maxwell equations of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] hold for $(E,B,\rho,J)$ if and only if

$$W\varphi-\partial_tG=\frac{\rho}{\varepsilon_0},\qquad WA+\nabla G=\mu_0J\qquad\text{on }\Omega\times I,$$

with $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ the constant of that postulate.

(b) [Gauge shift] If $\chi:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$ is a gauge function of class $C^2$ jointly on $\Omega\times I$ ([[def-em-gauge-transformation]]), then $G(T_\chi(\varphi,A))=G-W\chi$ on $\Omega\times I$ and the transformed pair has the same field pair $(E,B)$ ([[pthm-em-gauge-invariance]]); hence $T_\chi(\varphi,A)$ is in Lorenz gauge if and only if $W\chi=G$ on $\Omega\times I$.

(c) [Decoupling in Lorenz gauge] Suppose in addition that the given pair is in Lorenz gauge, $G=0$ on $\Omega\times I$. Then its field pair solves the sourced Maxwell system of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] if and only if the pair satisfies the decoupled sourced wave equations

$$W\varphi=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad WA=\mu_0J\qquad\text{on }\Omega\times I.$$

The two source-free equations $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$ hold automatically for every potential pair of class $C^2$. For an arbitrary given potential pair, the conjunction of Lorenz gauge with these two wave equations implies the sourced Maxwell system, but Maxwell's equations alone do not impose $G=0$ on that representative: their exact equivalent conditions remain the residual equations of (a), whose right-hand sides retain $\partial_tG$ and $\nabla G$.

(d) [Residual generators] If the $C^2$ gauge function of (b) satisfies $W\chi=0$ on $\Omega\times I$, then the transform of a pair in Lorenz gauge is again in Lorenz gauge and has the same field pair. When $\Omega$ is nonempty the Lorenz condition does not determine the pair: the generator $\chi(x,t)=x_1$, read in numerical SI components with gauge units as in [[def-em-gauge-transformation]], has $W\chi=0$ and changes $A$ by the nonzero constant vector $(1,0,0)$.

(e) [Scope] The identities and equivalences are properties of the given $C^2$ representation. No gauge function with $W\chi=G$, and no generator meeting prescribed initial or boundary values, is asserted to exist; that is a separate PDE conclusion with its own hypotheses, treated by the gauge-reachability theorem later on this page. No boundary, decay or initial condition on the pair is imposed, and no empirical claim or observability of $\varphi$ or $A$ is included. A pair of class $C^1$ defines $E$, $B$ and $G$ but need not possess the second derivatives appearing in $W\varphi$, $WA$, $\Delta$ or $\partial_tG$, so $C^2$ is the exact standing regularity here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), used through the cited published suppliers ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $c>0$, $t_0\in\mathbb R$, $T>t_0$, let $a,b\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ and let $h\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T])$ in the extension sense that $h$ is the restriction of a $C^\infty$ function on $\mathbb R^3\times J$ for some open interval $J\supset[t_0,T]$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). Write $W:=c^{-2}\partial_t^2-\Delta$, so that $c^2W=\Box_c$ is the wave operator of speed $c$ ([[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]], [[def-wave-equation-cauchy-data-and-wave-speed]]). For $\varphi\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ and $s\ge0$ let $H_\varphi(x,s):=s\,M_{cs}\varphi(x)$, where $M_r\varphi(x)=\frac{1}{4\pi}\int_{S^2}\varphi(x+rn)\,d\Omega(n)$ is the spherical mean of [[lem-em-spherical-mean-wave-identity]]. Define, with $s=t-t_0$, $$u(x,t):=\partial_sH_a(x,s)+H_b(x,s)+c^2\int_{t_0}^{t}H_{h(\cdot,v)}(x,t-v)\,dv,\qquad (x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T],$$ where $h(\cdot,v)$ denotes the map $x\mapsto h(x,v)$ and $\partial_sH_a$ is the partial derivative of $H_a$ in its second argument, evaluated at $s=t-t_0$. Then:

(a) $u$ is of class $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T]$ in the extension sense, $Wu=h$ on $\mathbb R^3\times(t_0,T)$ (indeed on the open neighbourhood of the closed time interval on which the extension of $h$ is defined), $u(\cdot,t_0)=a$ and $\partial_tu(\cdot,t_0)=b$.

(b) Uniqueness: every $v\in C^2(\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T])$ in the extension sense with $Wv=h$ on $\mathbb R^3\times(t_0,T)$, $v(\cdot,t_0)=a$ and $\partial_tv(\cdot,t_0)=b$ equals $u$.

(c) Domain of dependence: let $\tilde a,\tilde b\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$, $\tilde h\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T])$ and let $\tilde u$ be the corresponding solution. If $\tilde a=a$ and $\tilde b=b$ on the closed ball $\overline B_{c(t_*-t_0)}(x_*)$ and $\tilde h=h$ on the closed backward cone $K(x_*,t_*):=\{(y,v)\in\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,t_*]:|y-x_*|\le c(t_*-v)\}$ ([[def-forward-and-backward-wave-cones-domain-of-dependence-and-influence]]), then $\tilde u(x_*,t_*)=u(x_*,t_*)$ for every $x_*\in\mathbb R^3$ and $t_*\in[t_0,T]$.

(d) Compact support: if $a$ vanishes off a compact $K_a\subset\mathbb R^3$, $b$ vanishes off a compact $K_b$, and $h(\cdot,v)$ vanishes off a fixed compact $K_h$ for every $v\in[t_0,T]$, then for every $t\in[t_0,T]$ the function $u(\cdot,t)$ has compact spatial support: if $K_a\cup K_b\cup K_h\subseteq\overline B_\rho(0)$ for some $\rho>0$ (which exists, [[thm-heine-borel-rn]]), then $u(x,t)=0$ whenever $|x|>\rho+c(t-t_0)$.

No boundary condition on a finite spatial domain, no finite-total-energy hypothesis, and no decay of $a,b,h$ at infinity is assumed or asserted.

Adopt the SI system of units for this framework, with the following quantity
table and conventions; every symbol is a quantity of this framework and the
laboratory structure is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]].

(a) [Coordinates and constants] $x^0=ct$ and each spatial coordinate $x^i$
carries the metre (m); the time coordinate $t$ carries the second (s); the
conversion constant $c>0$ carries m s$^{-1}$ and has the exact SI defining
value $c=299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the elementary charge $e$ has the
exact SI defining value $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, and this
item does not assert that physical charge is quantised; the magnetic constant
$\mu_0>0$ carries N A$^{-2}$ and is measured, so no exact numerical value of
$\mu_0$ is asserted. The pre-2019 SI fixed the historical nominal
$\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}
=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took
effect on 20 May 2019, $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined. The SI brochure
quotes the nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption
with relative standard uncertainty $2.3\times10^{-10}$; this is historical
estimate and uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\mu_0$
or a current measured value. The electric constant is defined within the
framework by

$$\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$$

in F m$^{-1}$, consistent with the exact SI relation $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$,
so that $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ and $\varepsilon_0$ inherits the relative
standard uncertainty of $\mu_0$.

(b) [Electromagnetic quantities] Charge $q$ carries the coulomb (C); the
charge density $\rho$ of the framework's source definition carries C m$^{-3}$
and the current density $J$ carries A m$^{-2}$, so that the four-current
components $(c\rho,J)$ carry A m$^{-2}$; the electric field $E$ carries
V m$^{-1}$; the magnetic field $B$ carries the tesla (T), where
$1\ \mathrm{T}=1\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$; the scalar potential $\varphi$
carries V and the vector potential $A$ carries T m, so that the four-potential
components $(\varphi/c,A)$ carry T m; the components of the electromagnetic
two-form of the framework's tensor definition carry T; a force carries the
newton (N), $1\ \mathrm{N}=1\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$.

(c) [Mechanical quantities] A rest mass parameter $m$ carries the kilogram
(kg) and a four-momentum $P=mU$ of the relativistic particle model carries
kg m s$^{-1}$; field energy density carries J m$^{-3}$, energy flux
W m$^{-2}$, so that $1\ \mathrm{W}=1\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}=1\ \mathrm{V\,A}$.

(d) [Bookkeeping only] The unit of a quantity records the adopted system of
units; it does not show that a quantity is primitive in this or any other
framework, it contains no measurement, and it does not identify a quantity
with a similarly named quantity of another framework. The exact defining
values of $c$ and $e$ fix numerical conventions of the SI; they do not by
themselves identify $c$ with the vacuum propagation constant of ideal light,
which is the physical adoption of the framework's Minkowski postulate.

Let the laboratory region and its chart be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with
the units of [[def-em-si-conventions]].

(a) [Charge parameter] The framework takes a real **charge parameter**
$q\in\mathbb R$, measured in coulombs, attached to a source; its sign is the
sign of the source and it is a parameter of the model. Charge quantisation is
not asserted.

(b) [Smooth source fields] A **smooth (volume) source field** on
$\Omega\times I$ is a pair $(\rho,J)$ of maps $\rho:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$,
$J:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that is continuous on $\Omega\times I$ and of
class $C^1$ wherever a displayed equation differentiates it; $\rho$ is the
**frame charge density** (C m$^{-3}$) and $J$ the **frame current density**
(A m$^{-2}$). For each fixed $t\in I$ retain the compact Jordan branch: if
$V\subseteq\Omega$ is compact and Jordan measurable, define

$$Q_R(V,t):=\int_V\rho(y,t)dy$$

by [[def-riemann-integral-over-a-jordan-set]], with integrability supplied by
[[thm-continuous-functions-on-compact-jordan-sets-are-integrable]]. For the
full measurable-volume branch assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]),
as required by the published Lebesgue-measure interface. If $V$ is any bounded
Lebesgue-measurable subset with compact closure $\overline V\subseteq\Omega$,
define

$$Q(V,t):=\int_V\rho(y,t)d\lambda_3(y)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}F_t(y)\mathbf{1}_V(y)d\lambda_3(y),$$

where $F_t=\rho(\cdot,t)$ on $\Omega$ and $0$ elsewhere; the signed integral is
defined through its positive and negative parts
([[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]],
[[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]). The
function $F_t$ is Borel, and hence Lebesgue measurable: for every open
$O\subseteq\mathbb R$ its preimage inside the open set $\Omega$ is relatively
open in $\Omega$, hence open in $\mathbb R^3$, and the closed complement of
$\Omega$ is added precisely when $0\in O$
([[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]],
[[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]]). This integral is absolutely
finite: $\rho(\cdot,t)$ is bounded on the compact $\overline V$ by
[[thm-extreme-value-metric]], $V$ has finite Lebesgue measure by
[[prop-lebesgue-measure-is-sigma-finite-and-finite-on-bounded-sets]], and the
monotonicity and homogeneity of the nonnegative integral
([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]) bound
$\int|F_t|\mathbf{1}_Vd\lambda_3\le M_t\lambda_3(V)<\infty$, the indicator
integral being its simple-function value
([[prop-the-nonnegative-integral-agrees-with-the-simple-integral]]); the
positive and negative parts are measurable by
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]]. On
the compact Jordan branch, under the same Countable Choice assumption,
$Q=Q_R$ by [[lem-riemann-lebesgue-comparison-for-distribution-test-integrands]].
The
empty region has charge zero in both branches. The current flux remains
defined independently: for each oriented surface patch in $\Omega$ the current
flux at time $t$ is the surface integral of $J(\cdot,t)$ in the induced
orientation, as defined in [[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]].
Point sources and sheet sources are not source fields in this sense; they are
different objects, defined by their own pairings when the framework uses them.

(c) [Covariant identification] Write $j:=(c\rho,J)$, so $j^0=c\rho$ and
$j^i=J^i$. The framework adopts as a model premise the identification of the
charge-current of a source with a vector field of the affine Minkowski model,
and hence the component transformation law of
[[thm-sr-tensor-and-current-transformation]] for $j$ between inertial charts.
This is a model premise, not a theorem about physical currents.

(d) [Frame density, scalar multiplier and the normalized material branch]
Suppose additionally that the identified $j$ is $C^1$ and $j=\rho_0U$, with a
$C^1$ future timelike vector field $U$ and a $C^1$ real scalar multiplier
$\rho_0$. Since $U^0>0$, define the normalized chart direction $u:=U/U^0$, so
$u^0=1$, $u^i=U^i/U^0$. Then $j=(\rho_0U^0)u$ and, because the electromagnetic
convention is $j^0=c\rho$,

$$\rho=\rho_0U^0/c,\qquad J^i=\rho_0U^i=c\rho\,u^i.$$

Pointwise equality $\rho=\rho_0$ holds if and only if $\rho_0(U^0-c)=0$,
including the zero-multiplier case. Where $\rho_0\ne0$, equality is equivalent
to $U^0=c$, which does not alone imply $U^i=0$ for an arbitrary future timelike
$U$. Thus a scalar multiplier is not automatically a Lorentz rest charge
density. The direction $u$ is chart normalized, with no unit or
proper-four-velocity normalization imposed in this general branch; if its
coordinate velocity interpretation is adopted, the spatial velocity is
$v^i:=cu^i$.

For the separate convective source model, explicitly assume that $U$ is the
material proper-time four-velocity, normalized by $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$ as in
[[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]. This is an additional model
condition, not a consequence of the factorization $j=\rho_0U$. In that branch,
$U=\gamma(c,v)$, $|v|<c$, $\gamma=(1-|v|^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$, and

$$\rho=\gamma\rho_0,\qquad J=\rho v.$$

Here $\rho_0$ is the rest charge density of this stipulated convective model:
in a comoving inertial frame $U=(c,0,0,0)$ and $j=(c\rho_0,0,0,0)$. The
equality $\rho=\rho_0$ then holds exactly where $\rho_0=0$ or $v=0$
(equivalently $\gamma=1$). Both signs of charge and the zero-density case are
retained.

(e) [Scope] This definition fixes the source objects of the smooth branch and
their transformation interface. It asserts no conservation law (that is proved
for stated source classes) and no regularity of singular sources.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. If $f : V \to \mathbb C$ belongs to $L^1(\lambda_n)$,
then
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval and let $f:X\times I\to\mathbb C$
be such that:

1. for every $t\in I$, the function $x\mapsto f(x,t)$ is integrable;
2. for almost every $x$, the map $t\mapsto f(x,t)$ is differentiable on $I$;
3. for every $t\in I$, the function
   $$x\mapsto \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t),$$
   extended by zero where the derivative is undefined, is measurable;
4. there are a measurable null set $N$ and a nonnegative measurable function
   $g$ with
   $$\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$$
   and
   $$\left|\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t)\right|\le g(x)$$
   for every $t\in I$ and every $x\in X\setminus N$.

Then
$$F(t):=\int f(x,t)\,d\mu(x)$$
is differentiable on $I$, and
$$F'(t)=\int \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t)\,d\mu(x),$$
with the same zero extension in the last integral.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n \ge 1$,
let $S^{n-1} \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be the unit sphere, and let $\sigma$ be the
set function of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. Then $\sigma$
is a finite Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$, and for every Borel measurable
$f : \mathbb R^n \to [0,\infty]$,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n} f(x)\,d\lambda_n(x) = \int_0^\infty \int_{S^{n-1}} f(r\omega) r^{n-1}\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dr.$$
Moreover, $\sigma$ is the unique Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ with this
property.

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For $n\ge2$, a bounded $C^1$ domain Omega and $F\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^n)$, $\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}F\,dx=\int_{\partial\Omega}F\cdot\nu\,dS$. Both integrals are finite, with the continuous interior derivative convention and the outward normal on every boundary component.

**Set form.** Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, [[def-countable-choice]]), used to establish the Lebesgue measure space of [[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]. Let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be compact, Lebesgue measurable and of finite Lebesgue measure $\lambda_n(K)<\infty$, let $a<b$, and let $f$ be a real-valued function, defined and continuous together with its partial derivative $\partial_tf$ on an open neighbourhood of $K\times[a,b]$ in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$. Then $t\mapsto\int_Kf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x)$ is differentiable at every $t\in(a,b)$ with

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_Kf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x)=\int_K\partial_tf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x),$$

and at $t=a$ and $t=b$ it has relative (one-sided) derivatives, taken within $[a,b]$, both equal to the same displayed integral. Equivalently, for every $t\in[a,b]$ and every sequence $h_k\to0$ with $h_k\ne0$ and $t+h_k\in[a,b]$,

$$\lim_{k\to\infty}\frac{1}{h_k}\Bigl(\int_Kf(x,t+h_k)\,d\lambda_n(x)-\int_Kf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x)\Bigr)=\int_K\partial_tf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x).$$

**Surface form.** Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, [[def-countable-choice]]) for the surface measure of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]. Let $S$ be a fixed compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface in $\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge2$, and let $f$ be real-valued, defined and continuous together with $\partial_tf$ on an open neighbourhood of $S\times[a,b]$. Then $t\mapsto\int_Sf(\sigma,t)\,dS(\sigma)$ is differentiable in the same relative sense with

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_Sf(\sigma,t)\,dS(\sigma)=\int_S\partial_tf(\sigma,t)\,dS(\sigma).$$

The statements are pointwise in $t$ and make no claim about moving parameter sets $K(t)$ or $S(t)$, about singularities crossing $K$ or $S$, about differentiability of $\partial_tf$, or about differentiation in the spatial variables; only the one-dimensional parameter $t$ is differentiated. Integrals are Lebesgue integrals, and the surface integrals are those of the cited surface measure; the case $K=\varnothing$ or $\lambda_n(K)=0$ is included and the two sides vanish.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

Adopt as a physical assumption of this framework the following solution-selection rule for the classical vacuum model on the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with the constants and SI units of [[def-em-si-conventions]] (so $c>0$, $\mu_0>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$).

(a) [Formulation] In the potential formulation of [[pthm-em-lorenz-gauge-wave-form]] with the conventions of [[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]], for a $C^2$ potential pair in Lorenz gauge the sourced Maxwell system of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] is equivalent to the decoupled sourced wave equations $W\varphi=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $WA=\mu_0J$, where $W=c^{-2}\partial_t^2-\Delta$. The wave expression $W$ is invariant under $t\mapsto-t$; where explicit retarded or advanced constructions for a prescribed history exist, they give distinguished particular solutions built from the corresponding forward or backward fundamental kernels. Every other solution differs from a chosen particular solution by a source-free addition; retarded and advanced particular solutions also differ by such an addition. This describes the affine free-solution freedom, not a claim that arbitrary histories have exactly two solutions or that either construction always exists.

(b) [Adopted rule] The framework adopts the retarded branch with no free field added: the physical potential pair of the model is the retarded one, that is, the one whose support and propagation lie in the forward light cones of the source and which carries no field arriving from the past independently of the source. For the zero-incoming model the selected sourced solution has no independently prescribed homogeneous addition. If nonzero Cauchy data are instead prescribed, their compatible homogeneous addition is a separate initial-data model; it is not equivalent to setting every free addition to zero. The advanced construction and independent incoming free fields are excluded by the present retarded selection.

(c) [Status and scope] This is an adopted extra temporal condition carrying the model's arrow-of-time content. It is not a theorem, not a consequence of the time-symmetric wave or Maxwell equations (which admit advanced and free solutions as mathematical objects), and not a deduction from experiment; it asserts no existence, uniqueness, regularity, support or decay for any source class, all of which must be supplied separately by theorems of this page. It selects a solution only of the models to which it is applied; it introduces no product of distributions, no source model, no self-force, no radiation reaction, no measured signal and no statistical claim. The retarded compact-source branch to which this selection applies is developed on this page as a conditional theorem, and the point-source branch is developed later on this page; neither existence statement is part of this postulate. For the separately declared point-source branch assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), as in its exact source/field interfaces, and adopt the same no-free-addition retarded selection in the weak equations of [[post-em-distributional-vacuum-maxwell]], for the locally integrable field and proper point-current types of [[def-em-weak-sources]]. This extends the selection's model scope explicitly; neither existence nor an arbitrary convolution of noncompact distributions is postulated.

Adopt as a physical postulate of this framework the following four equations for
the fields of [[def-em-fields]] and the sources of [[def-em-sources]] on the
laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with
$\mu_0>0$, $c>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ and the SI units of
[[def-em-si-conventions]].

(a) [Smooth branch] Let $E,B$ be jointly $C^1$ fields with the additional
derivatives required by each equation existing and continuous, and let
$\rho,J$ be continuous. Then, with the divergence and curl of
[[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and the partial derivative
$\partial_t$ at fixed position of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]],

$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE.$$

(b) [Weak branch] Let instead $E,B$ be locally integrable $\mathbb R^3$-valued
fields and $\rho,J$ locally integrable scalar and vector fields on
$I\times\Omega$, identified with their regular distributions
([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]],
[[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]). Let
$\operatorname{div}$, $\operatorname{curl}$ and $\partial_t$ act as
distributional derivatives, componentwise, and let $\psi$ range over
$C_c^\infty(I\times\Omega)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]).
Then the same four identities hold in the sense of [[def-distribution]]: the
pairings

$$\langle\operatorname{div}E-\rho/\varepsilon_0,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{div}B,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{curl}E+\partial_tB,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{curl}B-\mu_0J-c^{-2}\partial_tE,\psi\rangle$$

all vanish for every such $\psi$, all derivatives being distributional
derivatives ([[def-distributional-derivative]]).

(c) [Scope] The postulate contains no magnetic charge: $\operatorname{div}B=0$
and no magnetic-source term appears in $\operatorname{curl}E$. Sources that
are not locally integrable functions (point or sheet sources) are covered by
neither branch and require their own definition. The equations are adopted
classical vacuum physics in the named inertial chart; they are not deduced from
charge conservation, from empirical agreement or from the special-relativity
postulates, and this item by itself asserts no covariance under changes of
inertial frame.

Let $U\cong I\times\Omega$ be the laboratory region of
[[def-em-lab-geometry]] with the constants and units of
[[def-em-si-conventions]], let $E,B$ be the fields of [[def-em-fields]] and
$\rho,J$ the source fields of [[def-em-sources]], with
$\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$.

(a) [Smooth branch] Let $E,B$ be jointly of class $C^2$ on $\Omega\times I$ and
$\rho,J$ of class $C^1$, and suppose the smooth branch of
[[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] holds with these fields and sources, in particular
$\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE$. Then the continuity equation

$$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0$$

holds pointwise on $\Omega\times I$, where $\operatorname{div}$ is the
divergence of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and
$\partial_t$ the partial time derivative of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

(b) [Distributional branch] Let $E,B,\rho,J$ be distributions on
$\Omega\times I$ ([[def-distribution]], [[def-distributional-derivative]]); in
particular they may be locally integrable fields and sources identified with
their regular distributions
([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]],
[[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]). Suppose the four
equations

$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE$$

hold in $\mathcal D'(\Omega\times I)$ with distributional derivatives. This
includes the original locally integrable weak branch of
[[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] and the separately adopted declared singular-source
models of [[post-em-distributional-vacuum-maxwell]], when their source and
field hypotheses hold. More generally the formal compatibility implication
applies to every distributional source pair for which the four identities
hold, without asserting physical adoption of arbitrary distributions. Then
$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0$ in $\mathcal D'(\Omega\times I)$.

source pair is compatible with the Maxwell equations, and by itself it proves
no conservation of physical charge. The derivative compatibility argument is
choice-free. An application to the declared singular-source model retains the
Countable Choice assumption of its defining source and surface-measure
formulation ([[def-countable-choice]]).

derivations.claim: Smoothness and wave equations. The source pair $(\rho,J)$ is jointly $C^\infty$ and vanishes outside the compact set $\overline B_a(0)\times[t_0,T]$, so $\rho/\varepsilon_0$ and each $h=\mu_0J_k$ belongs to $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R)$ [F5, F12]. Applying [F1] to these functions and using the identification $\varphi=\varepsilon_0^{-1}(K*\rho)$, $A_k=\mu_0(K*J_k)$ of the Given gives that $\varphi$ and every component of $A$ are of class $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$, with $W\varphi=\rho/\varepsilon_0$ and $WA=\mu_0J$ pointwise. This is (a).

Derivative identities for the retarded kernel. Fix $h\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R)$. For fixed $(x,t)$ the change of variable $y\mapsto z=x-y$, a $C^1$ diffeomorphism of $\mathbb R^3$ with $|\det D(x-\cdot)|=1$, is legitimate for the integrable function $y\mapsto h(y,t-|x-y|/c)/(4\pi|x-y|)$ [F6], so $(K*h)(x,t)=\int h(x-z,t-|z|/c)/(4\pi|z|)\,dz$. Choose $b_h>0$ such that the spatial projection of $\operatorname{supp}h$ lies in $\overline B_{b_h}(0)$, and let $M_h$ be a finite global bound on the first derivatives of $h$ (they are continuous and compactly supported). On a parameter neighbourhood $|x|<R$, $|t|<R$, with $R>0$, each differentiated integrand vanishes unless $|x-z|\le b_h$, hence unless $|z|<R+b_h$. Its absolute value is bounded by $M_h\mathbf1_{B_{R+b_h+1}}(z)/(4\pi|z|)$, which is integrable by [F8]. The zero extension at $z=0$ affects a null set only; this majorant is independent of the parameter being differentiated. The derivative is measurable as a limit of measurable difference quotients, so [F7] applies once per parameter $x_1,x_2,x_3,t$ with the other three parameters held fixed, and gives $\partial_{x_i}(K*h)=K*(\partial_{y_i}h)$ and $\partial_t(K*h)=K*(\partial_th)$ on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$, where $\partial_{y_i}h$ is the partial derivative of $h$ in its $i$-th spatial argument.

No field before the source. Suppose $t<t_0$. For every $y$ the retarded argument satisfies $t-|x-y|/c\le t<t_0$, where $\rho$ and $J$ vanish identically by the support hypothesis; hence both integrands in the definitions of $\varphi$ and $A$ vanish for every $y$, and $\varphi(x,t)=0$, $A(x,t)=0$ [F9]. Therefore $E=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA=0$ and $B=\nabla\times A=0$ at every event with $t<t_0$, which is (d).

Total charge. By the support hypothesis, $Q(t)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\rho(y,t)dy=\int_{B_a(0)}\rho(y,t)dy$ for every $t$, and $Q(t)=0$ for $t<t_0$; the integral depends smoothly on $t$ with $Q'(t)=\int_{B_a(0)}\partial_t\rho(y,t)dy$ by [F11] applied to the fixed compact $\overline B_a(0)$ (the integrals over the open and closed balls agree since the smooth source vanishes on the boundary) (the integrands $\rho,\partial_t\rho$ are continuous on a neighbourhood of $\overline B_a(0)\times[t-1,t+1]$) [F5, F12]. Fix $t$ and $R>a$; the continuity equation and the divergence theorem [F10] give $\int_{B_a(0)}\operatorname{div}J(y,t)dy=\int_{B_R(0)}\operatorname{div}J(y,t)dy=\int_{\partial B_R(0)}J(y,t)\cdot\nu\,dS=0$, because $J$ vanishes outside $\overline B_a(0)$ and $R>a$; hence $Q'(t)=-\int_{B_a(0)}\operatorname{div}J(y,t)dy=0$. Thus $Q$ is constant on $\mathbb R$ and, being zero at times before $t_0$, is identically zero, which is (f).

Lorenz gauge. By step 1.2 applied to each component $J_i$ and to $\rho$, together with linearity of the integral [F9], $$\operatorname{div}A=\mu_0\sum_{i=1}^{3}\partial_{x_i}(K*J_i)=\mu_0\sum_{i=1}^{3}K*(\partial_{y_i}J_i)=\mu_0\,K*(\operatorname{div}J),\qquad c^{-2}\partial_t\varphi=c^{-2}\varepsilon_0^{-1}K*(\partial_t\rho)=\mu_0\,K*(\partial_t\rho),$$ the second equality using $c^{-2}\varepsilon_0^{-1}=\mu_0$ [F4]. Adding, $G=\operatorname{div}A+c^{-2}\partial_t\varphi=\mu_0K*(\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J)=0$ pointwise on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ by the assumed continuity equation and linearity of the kernel integral [F9]. This is (b); continuity is also used in step 1.4 to establish the total-charge conclusion.

Zero-data Cauchy identification. Fix $t_1<t_0$ and $T'>t_0$. By step 1.3, $\varphi(\cdot,t_1)=0$, $A(\cdot,t_1)=0$ and also $\partial_t\varphi(\cdot,t_1)=0$, $\partial_tA(\cdot,t_1)=0$ (the same vanishing argument applies to the time derivatives, whose integrands contain $\rho_t,J_t$, vanishing for retarded arguments $<t_0$ as well). By step 1.1 the pair is $C^\infty$, hence $C^2$, on $\mathbb R^3\times[t_1,T']$ in the extension sense and satisfies $W\varphi=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $WA=\mu_0J$ on $\mathbb R^3\times(t_1,T')$; [F3] (with its final time renamed $T'$ and its Cauchy data $a=b=0$) therefore identifies each component with the zero-data solution constructed there. As $T'>t_0$ is arbitrary, the identification extends to $\mathbb R^3\times[t_1,\infty)$, which is (e).

Maxwell fields. $E$ and $B$ are $C^\infty$ because $\varphi$ and $A$ are [step 1.1, F12]. By [F2] with the Lorenz divergence $G$ of step 2.1, $\operatorname{div}E=W\varphi-\partial_tG=\rho/\varepsilon_0-0$ and $\operatorname{curl}B-c^{-2}\partial_tE=WA+\nabla G=\mu_0J+0$; the two source-free equations $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$ are automatic for the potential pair [F2]. Hence the smooth branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] holds for $(E,B,\rho,J)$ on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ with $E,B$ of class $C^\infty$, which is (c). The remaining clause (g) is scope bookkeeping: every hypothesis used above is one of the displayed compact smooth source hypotheses, no point, line, sheet or distributional source is involved, no product of distributions or self-field is formed, no finite-energy, decay, self-force or measurement claim is made, and the only choice assumption is $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ carried by the kernel, polar and Cauchy suppliers.

boundaries.evidence: Statement/Definition and its cited interfaces: The hypotheses fix a>0 and t_0<T, so the source support contained in the closed ball times [t_0,T] is nonempty as a prescription; the empty-source instance rho=J=0 gives phi=A=0 by the retarded integrals and every clause holds trivially through steps 1.1 and 3.1.

Zero sources and zero Cauchy data are covered: step 1.3 proves phi=A=0 and E=B=0 for t<t_0, step 2.2 identifies the pair with the zero-data Cauchy solution of [F3] at every t_1<t_0, and the zero total charge is step 1.4.

boundaries.reason: No cardinality-one index set occurs: the retarded integrals run over R^3, the charge coordinate is summed over the three spatial indices in step 2.1, and charge is not asserted to be quantised.

boundaries.evidence: Step 1.2 uses an integrable M_h*1_{B_(R+b_h+1)}/(4*pi*|z|) majorant covering the full spatial support of an arbitrary compact h, with the singleton zero extension.

The source is restricted to the compact time interval [t_0,T]; step 1.3 computes the fields before t_0, step 2.2 uses the extension-sense convention at t_1<t_0 with [F3], and [F1] supplies smoothness and W(K*h)=h on the whole space.

AC_omega is assumed in the Statement and is carried by the kernel, polar-coordinate and Cauchy suppliers [F1,F8,F3]; steps 1.2 and 1.4 invoke the countably additive measure interface through those facts.

boundaries.reason: No equivalence is asserted by clauses (a)-(g); the only 'if and only if' used inside the proof is the Lorenz-gauge decoupling criterion quoted in [F2], an imported supplier statement used one-way in step 3.1.
There is no converse implication of the theorem to check; clause (e)'s identification is the uniqueness direction supplied by [F3], and clause (f) is a direct identity.

risk_review.notes: Checked all seven steps against kernel(b), compact parameter integral, differentiation-under-integral, Cauchy uniqueness and Lorenz equivalence interfaces. Compact smooth h belongs to C_c^infty, and the translated-variable first derivatives admit the integrable |z|^-1 bound on B_(R+b_h+1), including the kernel singleton as a null exclusion. Closed-ball parameter integration on nondegenerate time windows and divergence over R>a give Q_prime=0; early-time support gives Q=0. Derivative transfer and epsilon0*mu0*c²=1 give G=0, then all Maxwell identities. Early-time zero derivatives meet extension-sense Cauchy data on each finite slab, hence uniqueness on the half-line. Amended Statement(b): continuity is used both for gauge and total charge, as the proof already states; made the compact-parameter time window explicit. Reader repairs are sound; no singular source or finite-energy conclusion is inferred.
